items.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: we’ve been with Ed Shaughnessy here for a couple of days

ctx.x: I’ll say black if you say black, all right?

Okay that’s cool. But a lot of black people I think have the church as their foundation and I was often, all the time in church, because my father was the choir director. And so I didn’t really have a choice in terms of the singing thing. And also when nobody wanted to take a particular solo, then my father said you’ve got to sing the tenor solo, or the baritone. I was both because he lacked tenors and he lacked baritones. So that’s where I think my first performing thing started to really come into effect. And…

performing thing. But I wasn’t one of those kids that was pushed on stage at all. You know it’s just a nurturing of a love. You know my family had so much music and music became like an integral part of our lives, and I learned very early on, as you spoke about how you had the radio under your pillow, you know many nights, and it’s the same with me. When I was growing up they first had those little cassette tape recorders that you could buy at Radio Shack. They were real poor quality, but actually we’ve been with…

items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Byron has them. He thinks they’re great Basie records... That’s what Byron likes about it.

ctx.x: Or the names of the musicians weren’t on.

Oh yes. If I might interject it’s annoyed me that the two best albums I made with Basie were called “Broadway Basie’s Way,” and “Hollywood Basie’s Way,” two separate albums on Command Records. Byron has them. He thinks they’re great Basie records, ‘cause Roy Eldridge was on one of them. And they have taken them both, and they’ve put them, I think Decca bought them up, and they’ve put them into a double album. I’m not talking CD now, I’m talking about LP. And a couple of years ago I spotted it in a store called…

me playing.” He said “I thought it was Sonny Payne.” I says “that’s a nice compliment, but no that’s me, I made “‘Strangers in the Night.’” So they have no idea whether it’s me, and for people that don’t know Lockjaw Davis, who was a great tenor player at the time with the band, they won’t know it’s Roy Eldridge unless they know their jazz history. So I’m giving a very long answer I hope you don’t mind but you’re absolutely right, when they don’t list personnel, and they don’t even list the period of time when it…
